beats.caption: A cache miss sends a read out to memory
beats.text: When data is not in the GPU's caches, a read request leaves the die for an HBM stack. Every thread that needs that data waits until it comes back. Memory latency is that round-trip time.

beats.caption: First the request waits in the memory controller
beats.text: The controller holds a queue of requests and reorders them to reuse open rows and avoid bank conflicts. Under heavy load this queueing can be the largest piece of the delay.

beats.caption: Inside the DRAM: open the row, then read the column
beats.text: If the row is closed the chip needs ACTIVATE (tRCD, about 14 ns) and then a column read (CAS latency, about 14 ns more). A row that another request left open costs a PRECHARGE on top.

beats.caption: Then the data rides back; the total is around 100 ns
beats.text: Add the bus or link trip both ways and the result is typically 80-120 ns for local DRAM, hundreds of GPU clock cycles. GPUs hide it by keeping thousands of threads in flight.

beats.caption: Bandwidth is not latency
beats.text: A system can move terabytes per second and still stall on each miss: bandwidth is how wide the pipe is, latency is how long it is. CXL memory adds capacity but also adds a link hop, often 100+ ns more. Related: Micron (MU), Astera Labs (ALAB), Intel (INTC).
